title: How many partitions should a topic have, what are the real constraints, and why can you never decrease partition count?
shortTitle: How many partitions should a topic have, what are the real constraints, and why can you never decrease partition count?

s1_definition.profdef: The partition count sets the maximum parallelism for a topic because within a consumer group a partition is consumed by at most one consumer, so the number of partitions caps how many consumers can work in parallel. You size it from target throughput divided by per-partition throughput, with headroom for growth, while respecting constraints like total partitions per broker, open file handles, memory for the page cache, rebalance and metadata overhead, and end-to-end latency. You can increase partitions later but never decrease them, because shrinking would require moving or deleting data and, critically, would break key-based ordering since the hash-to-partition mapping would change.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of partitions as the number of teller counters at National Bank of India. More counters let more tellers serve customers at once, so you size the counters to the expected rush. But there is a limit to how many counters one branch building can hold without chaos. And once you have assigned customers to counters by the first letter of their surname, you cannot suddenly remove counters, because then customers who were always served at counter five would scatter, breaking the orderly queue history you promised each customer.
s1_definition.oneliner: Partitions are the parallelism dial sized by throughput with headroom, bounded by broker and latency limits, and you can only add them, never remove them, because removal would break key ordering and strand data.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The partition count sets the maximum parallelism for a topic because within a consumer group a partition is consumed by at most one consumer, so the number of partitions caps how many consumers can work in parallel. You size it from target throughput divided by per-partition throughput, with headroom for growth, while respecting constraints like total partitions per broker, open file handles, memory for the page cache, rebalance and metadata overhead, and end-to-end latency. You can increase partitions later but never decrease them, because shrinking would require moving or deleting data and, critically, would break key-based ordering since the hash-to-partition mapping would change.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of partitions as the number of teller counters at National Bank of India. More counters let more tellers serve customers at once, so you size the counters to the expected rush. But there is a limit to how many counters one branch building can hold without chaos. And once you have assigned customers to counters by the first letter of their surname, you cannot suddenly remove counters, because then customers who were always served at counter five would scatter, breaking the orderly queue history you promised each customer.

**One line to remember:** Partitions are the parallelism dial sized by throughput with headroom, bounded by broker and latency limits, and you can only add them, never remove them, because removal would break key ordering and strand data.

sections.s2_technical:
Partition count matters most because it caps consumer parallelism. In one consumer group a partition is owned by exactly one consumer, so a topic with six partitions can have at most six actively consuming instances in a group; a seventh sits idle. So you pick partitions based on how much parallel consuming you will ever need, not just today.

The sizing formula is practical. You estimate target throughput, say sixty megabytes per second, and the throughput a single partition sustains for your consumers, say ten megabytes per second limited by downstream processing. Dividing gives six partitions as a floor, and you add headroom, often doubling, to allow future consumer scaling without a repartition. The same reasoning applies to message rate rather than bytes if your bottleneck is records per second.

The constraints are real. Each partition replica is a set of files on a broker, so more partitions mean more open file handles and more memory for index and page cache. A broker has a practical ceiling on total partitions, often in the low thousands per broker depending on version and hardware, and the cluster has a ceiling in the tens to low hundreds of thousands. Too many partitions also slow down controller operations, lengthen rebalances, and increase end-to-end latency because the producer spreads batches thinner so each batch fills more slowly. More partitions also increase the time to recover after a broker failure because more leader elections must happen.

You increase partitions with a command like `kafka-topics --alter --topic transfers --partitions 12`. But you can never decrease them, for two reasons. First, Kafka would have to physically move or delete the data in the removed partitions, and there is no safe general way to merge partition logs. Second and more important, producers map a key to a partition using a hash of the key modulo the partition count. If you change the partition count, the same key now maps to a different partition, which breaks the guarantee that all of one key's records live in one partition in order. Even increasing partitions has this subtle effect: new records for an existing key may land in a different partition than the old ones, so if strict per-key ordering across all time matters, you plan the partition count carefully up front or use a custom partitioner that is stable.

A senior nuance is that over-partitioning to be safe is itself a cost, because it hurts latency and recovery and wastes resources. The better practice is to size with reasonable headroom, monitor consumer lag and broker partition counts, and add partitions deliberately when scaling, accepting that you may temporarily relax per-key ordering during the transition. For keyed topics where ordering is sacred, such as per-account transaction streams, you treat the partition count as effectively fixed and size it generously at design time.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India creates a `transactions` topic that keys events by account so all of one customer's events stay ordered. The platform team must choose a partition count that supports current and future volume without ever needing to shrink.

Problem 1 — if they pick too few partitions, they cannot scale the fraud-detection consumer group beyond that many instances, so during a traffic surge the group cannot keep up and lag grows. This is exactly why partition count caps parallelism.

Problem 2 — if they pick an enormous number to be safe, broker file handles, memory, and rebalance times suffer, and latency rises. This is exactly the constraint tradeoff.

Problem 3 — someone later wants to reduce partitions to save resources, not realizing that Rajesh's events, which always went to partition three, would suddenly scatter and lose their ordering history. This is exactly why you can never decrease partition count.

The code will show a small sizing helper that computes a recommended partition count from throughput, demonstrate the key-to-partition hashing so the reader sees why changing the count reshuffles keys, and log the result for Rajesh and Priya.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the sizing demo
java -cp target/partition-sizing-service-1.0.0.jar \
  com.bank.partitions.PartitionSizingDemo

# Increase partitions (allowed); decreasing is not supported by Kafka
kafka-topics --bootstrap-server broker1:9092 --alter \
  --topic transactions --partitions 24
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a sizing request of sixty megabytes per second target, ten megabytes per second per partition, and a doubling headroom; plus two accounts, SAV2001 and CUR3001.

Step 1 — the planner divides sixty by ten to get a floor of six partitions, then multiplies by the headroom factor of two to recommend twelve partitions. This gives room for the consumer group to grow to twelve instances later.

Step 2 — the planner computes the partition for each account using hash of key modulo partition count. With twelve partitions, SAV2001 lands in one specific partition and CUR3001 in another, and all of each customer's events will always go there, preserving order.

Step 3 — the planner recomputes with six partitions and shows that the same accounts now map to different partitions. This visibly demonstrates that changing the count reshuffles keys, which would scatter a customer's ordered history.

Step 4 — the planner's validate method is asked to go from twelve to six partitions and rejects it with an exception, because decreasing would strand data and break key ordering.

```
2026-10-24 22:10:01 [INFO] Recommended partition count: 12
2026-10-24 22:10:01 [INFO] SAV2001 → partition 9 (with 12) but 3 (with 6) — shrinking reshuffles keys!
2026-10-24 22:10:01 [INFO] CUR3001 → partition 4 (with 12) but 1 (with 6) — shrinking reshuffles keys!
2026-10-24 22:10:01 [SEVERE] Rejected repartition: Cannot decrease partitions from 12 to 6: would strand data and break key-based ordering
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Sizing input: target=60 MB/s, per-partition=10 MB/s, headroom=2x
    │
    ▼
  PartitionPlanner.recommendPartitions()
    │ floor = ceil(60/10) = 6
    │ recommended = 6 × 2 = 12
    ▼
  topic transactions: 12 partitions  (max 12 consumers per group)

  Key mapping (why you cannot shrink):
    SAV2001 ─hash mod 12→ partition 9    ┐ 12 → 6 would move
    SAV2001 ─hash mod 6 → partition 3    ┘ Rajesh's events elsewhere
    CUR3001 ─hash mod 12→ partition 4    ┐ breaking per-key order
    CUR3001 ─hash mod 6 → partition 1    ┘

  Repartition guard:
    12 → 24 allowed (add parallelism)
    12 → 6 rejected (strand data + break ordering)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The partition count is the parallelism dial for a topic, because inside a consumer group each partition is read by at most one consumer, so the number of partitions is the ceiling on how many instances can consume in parallel. I size it from throughput: I take the target throughput and divide by what a single partition can sustain given the downstream processing, then I add headroom, usually doubling, so the consumer group can scale later without a repartition.

The constraints are real and I respect them. Every partition is files on a broker, so more partitions mean more open file handles and more memory for indexes and page cache. There is a practical ceiling on partitions per broker and per cluster, and too many partitions lengthen rebalances, slow controller operations, raise end-to-end latency because batches fill more slowly, and slow recovery after a broker failure. So over-partitioning to be safe is itself a cost.

You can increase partitions with an alter command, but you can never decrease them. There are two reasons. Physically, Kafka has no safe way to merge partition logs, so shrinking would strand or require deleting data. More importantly, producers map a key to a partition by hashing the key modulo the partition count, so changing the count makes the same key map to a different partition, which breaks the guarantee that all of one key's records live in one ordered partition.

In my National Bank of India project, the transactions topic was keyed by account so every customer's events stayed ordered in one partition. We sized it generously up front with headroom and treated the count as effectively fixed, because reducing it would have scattered customers like Rajesh across partitions and destroyed their ordered transaction history. When we needed more parallelism we added partitions deliberately and accepted a brief relaxation of per-key ordering during the transition.
